events.text: {npc}, a cloud-ferry pilot with wind-cracked hands, moors beside you at the Lantern Landing and does not wait to be asked. "Ninth Orchard Isle is sinking," {he} says. "A hand-breadth a night. The steward says weather. I have flown that air ten years, and weather never did that."

choices.text: Walk the landing and hear it all

mem.note: was heard out at the landing

effects.log: By the end of the walk you are curious, and {npc} has stopped gripping the mooring line.

choices.text: Ask what the steward says

effects.log: "Weather," {npc} says flatly. "Every night, the same weather."

choices.text: Say isles have always sunk and risen

effects.log: {npc} unties the line and casts off without a word.

events.text: You and {npc} anchor a kite above Ninth Orchard Isle and mark its rim against one fixed star, night after night. The isle never wobbles or lurches. It drops, a finger's width, then a hand's, steady as a rope being paid out.

choices.text: Mark the rim again at dawn

effects.log: The same drop, to the hair. Whatever is doing this is patient.

choices.text: Let {npc} fly the night watch alone

effects.log: {npc} keeps the watch and brings back a tally cold and exact.

events.text: Under the root-mass of the isle four hollow cradles hang open to the wind, each the size of a rice jar. In each lies a grey pebble painted to glint like jade. {npc} lowers the lantern with a shaking hand. "Lift-stone cradles," {he} says. "Someone left them holding gravel."

choices.text: Scrape a pebble with your thumbnail

effects.log: The paint flakes off grey. It is plain river gravel.

choices.text: Climb back before the steward looks down

effects.log: You leave every pebble where it lies. Nobody must know you were here yet.

events.text: The steward of Ninth Orchard Isle keeps neat accounts. In them {npc} finds a standing debt to a Phoenix House broker, two years of interest on spirit stones, and the payments stop the month the first cradle was emptied. {npc} reads the page twice. "The stones were not stolen," {he} says slowly. "They were sold."

choices.text: Copy the page

effects.log: You copy the sums in your own hand. Numbers do not lie as well as stewards.

choices.text: Ask who the broker is

effects.log: A smooth-handed broker of the Vermilion Phoenix House, with a stall at the Sky Market.

events.text: On the steward's own landing, with {npc} beside you, you say it aloud: the lift-stones were sold to pay a debt, and painted gravel hung in their place. The isle's families gather and say nothing for a long moment. Then the steward sits down on a crate and weeps.

choices.text: Ask for the stones back, not the steward's ruin

mem.note: saw you spare a weeping steward

effects.log: The broker is made to sell the stones back at what was paid. Ninth Orchard climbs a hand-breadth a night until it rides high again.

choices.text: Lay the case before the Jade Court

effects.log: The Court orders the stones recovered and the steward's post forfeit. The isle rises, and your name is read aloud at the hearing.

events.text: Your answer goes round the isle's ladders by nightfall, and it is the wrong one. A blameless gardener is shunned at the well; a whale-watcher is shouted off the dock. {npc} finds you after. "It was not that," {he} says quietly. "I flew under the whole isle. Nothing was feeding on it."

choices.text: Apologise at the well, loudly

effects.log: You say you were wrong where the whole isle can hear. It helps a little.

choices.text: Go back under the isle and think again

effects.log: You go over every cradle and every pebble again. Somewhere in them is what you missed.

events.text: Three nights of marking the rim, and a storm scatters the stars. The tally is spoiled, and {npc} sits in the lee of the kite with the ruined chart across {his} knees. "We begin again," {he} says, "when the sky clears."

choices.text: Agree to wait

effects.log: You write down everything you have so far, so the waiting loses none of it.

choices.text: Fly the clear gap between storms

effects.log: One clear hour, no more. But you know the isle's outline by heart now.

events.text: A line snaps while you are under the isle. You swing into the root-mass and come back up scraped and shaking, and {npc} winds the rope in hand over hand, scolding the whole time.

choices.text: Let {npc} scold

effects.log: You let {him}. It is a kind of care.

choices.text: Insist you are fine

effects.log: You are not fine. {npc} knows it, and says nothing.

events.text: {npc}, a warden of the White Stairs who counts climbers for the Jade Court, catches your sleeve at the foot of the steps. "You trod the nine-thousandth step and it hummed," {he} says. "It hums for no one. Not in sixty years." Your boot found that step as though it had always known where it was.

choices.text: Tread it again to be sure

effects.log: It hums again, low and clear, under your boot alone.

choices.text: Ask who it hummed for last

effects.log: "Nobody who is recorded," {npc} says, and looks away.

choices.text: Say it is old jade settling

effects.log: {npc} lets go of your sleeve. A warden knows the difference between settling and singing.

events.text: On the nine-thousandth step the jade sings under your boot and under no other. {npc} tries a bell-weight, then a heavier one, then the warden's own foot. Nothing wakes it but you. Far up the white stair, climbers stop and look down to see who has set the stone singing.

choices.text: Kneel and lay a palm on the step

effects.log: The jade is warm, as if someone had only just stood up from it.

choices.text: Let {npc} keep the climbers moving

mem.note: kept the stairs quiet for you

effects.log: {npc} shoos the curious past with great dignity and no explanation.

events.text: The wardens' counting-books are bound in blue cloth and smell of camphor. In a volume from an age ago {npc} finds one climber logged at step 9,999 and then never again: no ascent, no fall, no name. Beside the line is a cinnabar thumbprint, small and deliberate. {npc} touches it and says nothing.

choices.text: Copy the line and the print

effects.log: You copy both with a fine brush. The print is the harder part.

choices.text: Ask the old warden-clerk who wrote it

effects.log: The clerk's successor's successor shrugs. "Wardens write what they see," {npc} translates, gently.

events.text: The archive holds a vow-scroll sealed with the same cinnabar whorls. {npc} lays your thumb beside the print, gently, as one lays a leaf on a leaf. The whorls agree. The scroll's last line is dated the year before you were born. The last piece is not here: whoever could say what happened on that step has not come back to it yet.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to keep the scroll safe

effects.log: {npc} promises to keep it, and the copy, and the line from the book. "For whoever comes to this step," {he} says.

choices.text: Burn a stick of incense at the foot of the stairs

effects.log: The smoke goes straight up, which the wardens call a good sign.

events.text: You are new to these stairs, and still your boot stops at the nine-thousandth step before you look down. At the foot waits {npc}, who studies you a long time. "A warden left this in our rolls for whoever came back to that step," {he} says. "I was told you would look as though you already knew the way."

choices.text: Take the warden's roll

effects.log: A cinnabar thumbprint, a date, a note: the stairs kept a place, and the place is yours.

choices.text: Ask who the warden was

effects.log: "My teacher's teacher," {npc} says. "They said you would ask that first."

events.text: At the foot of the White Stairs, with {npc} beside you, you say it plainly: the print was yours, from the life before this one. You climbed to step 9,999, turned back to carry a failing climber down, and the stairs kept your place. {npc} lays a hand flat on the first step. "The stone was waiting," {he} says. "I only counted."

choices.text: Climb the last step with {npc} beside you

mem.note: climbed the last step with you

effects.log: The ten-thousandth step is only a step. You stand on it a long time, and nobody hurries you.

choices.text: Carry a flagging pilgrim down, as you once did

effects.log: The pilgrim does not know why you are weeping. The wardens do, and bow.

events.text: "A jealous climber's curse," you said, or "a warden's trick for favours," and the stairs are loud with it. A pilgrim is shouted off the steps; a warden is struck from the rolls for a week. {npc} is not angry. "That hum is not a trick," {he} says. "It is older than favours."

choices.text: Speak for the warden at the Jade Court

effects.log: You go in person and say you were wrong. The warden is reinstated.

choices.text: Stand on the humming step and think

effects.log: You stand there till dark. The jade hums, and says nothing more.

events.text: A week at the humming step, and you learn only that the jade is patient. Climbers begin to leave offerings on it. {npc} sweeps them off each dusk. "The trail goes cold," {he} says. "Stone does not hurry for anyone."

choices.text: Wait it out

effects.log: You note every hour the stone hummed and every hour it did not.

choices.text: Come back at the new moon

effects.log: Different light, same silence. But you know the step better.

events.text: You ask the wardens one question too many, and the oldest of them closes the books. {npc} winces. "A warden's patience is a thing you spend," {he} says, "and you just spent a year of it."

choices.text: Make it right with the oldest warden

effects.log: You bring tea and say nothing about the books. It is noticed.

choices.text: Let it lie and move on

effects.log: Some doors close. Others stay open a crack.

events.text: {npc}, a junior clerk of the Jade Court with ink to the wrists, finds you in the arcade of the Court and sets a fascicle on the bench between you. "Immortal Ryeon of the Frost Moon House," {he} says, "has every line a life earns. Except one. Nobody will tell me why the first line is missing."

choices.text: Read the fascicle with {npc}

effects.log: Fifty pages of honours. One missing line, and one page of newer paper than the rest.

choices.text: Ask why {npc} brings it to you

effects.log: "Because the Court will not look," {npc} says. "You might."

choices.text: Say a ledger gap is a clerk's error

effects.log: {npc} gathers the fascicle and goes without arguing.

events.text: Ryeon's entry in the Lotus Ledger lists a wedding, a hundred honours, a seat at the Frost Moon table. The first line, birth and parentage, is simply not there. {npc} shows you the page. It is the only one in the fascicle on fresh paper, and its ink is a shade too even.

choices.text: Hold the page to the lamp

effects.log: Faint lines of an older hand ghost behind the new ink: something was scraped out.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to fetch the neighbouring years

effects.log: {npc} fetches them. Every one of them is complete.

events.text: The Keeper's retired under-clerk farms a cloud no bigger than a barn and keeps the kettle on. After the second pot, the old clerk stops pretending. "A Frost Moon steward," the old clerk says, "paid twice the fee to tidy a line. I was told not to read what I tidied. I did not."

choices.text: Thank the old clerk and keep the secret

effects.log: The old clerk's shoulders drop. "Somebody had to ask," the clerk says.

choices.text: Ask what the steward looked like

effects.log: A tall, careful steward with a nervous cough. Frost Moon House kept very few of those.

events.text: The Frost Moon nursery rolls are kept in a cold stone room under the house. {npc}, thanks to your faction's seal, is let in. The rolls show a foundling taken from a salvage-ship and entered as "the heir" in the very month the house's only heir died of a fever. {npc} sits down on the cold floor. "They did not erase a birth," {he} says. "They erased a swap."

choices.text: Copy the nursery page

effects.log: You copy it. A house may keep its shames, but not from a determined clerk.

choices.text: Leave the rolls exactly as found

effects.log: You close the book and leave the cold room as you found it.

events.text: In the Court's reading room, with {npc} beside you and Immortal Ryeon in the third row, you lay it out: a dead heir, a foundling, a steward's careful fee, a line scraped out of the Ledger. Ryeon does not move. When it is done, Ryeon stands and says only, quietly, "I always wondered why they never spoke of my cradle."

choices.text: Ask the Court to add a true first line

mem.note: saw you give a foundling a true line

effects.log: The Court writes it in: "foundling, salvage-ship, raised in love." Ryeon asks for the brush, and signs it alone.

choices.text: Let the Court have the scandal

effects.log: The steward is censured, the house fined in precedence. Your name goes round the Court as the one who read the margins.

events.text: The Court answers your accusation with a formal letter, and the Frost Moon House with a very cold bow. "You named a fox spirit or a sovereign," {npc} says, holding the Court's censure, "and I put my name to it." {He} is not angry. {He} is tired, which is worse.

choices.text: Take the censure on yourself

effects.log: You write to the Court yourself. The censure on {npc} is lifted.

choices.text: Go back to the margins

effects.log: A scraped line, a swapped cradle. You read them until the lamp is low.

events.text: You ask for the same fascicle a third time, and the Court's archivist reads aloud a rule about idle petitions. The reading room is half full. {npc} goes red to the ears for you. "Perhaps," {he} says, "we should have read it less loudly."

choices.text: Laugh at the archivist's rule

effects.log: You laugh louder than the archivist. The reading room forgives you.

choices.text: Be quieter next time

effects.log: The Court forgets in a season. You do not.

events.text: The old clerk's cloud is steep and the path to it worse. You come down with a twisted wrist and a lecture from {npc}, who has packed a poultice and no patience. "Next time," {he} says, "we ask the clerk to come down."

choices.text: Take the poultice

effects.log: You take it. {npc} ties it on with a knot that will outlast the wrist.

choices.text: Say it is nothing

effects.log: It is not nothing. {npc} lets you say it anyway.

events.text: {npc}, a bell-apprentice not yet twenty, with chalk on {his} cuffs and a first grey hair, pulls you into the shadow of the temple. "The great bell rang again," {he} says. "Nobody touched it. It rang an hour before the storm gate opened, and again an hour before the last one. I am the only one who has noticed."

choices.text: Go up the bell-tower with {npc}

effects.log: You climb the ladders together. At the top the bell hangs silent, patient, enormous.

choices.text: Ask how many storms it has rung before

effects.log: "Nine," {npc} says. "I counted. Nine."

choices.text: Say bells ring in wind

effects.log: {npc} looks at the still air and then at you, and goes.

events.text: You and {npc} keep vigil under the great bell through the longest night of the storm season. At the third watch the bell tolls, one deep note, and nobody is near it. But the rope twitches a full heartbeat before the clapper moves, as if it had been pulled from somewhere else.

choices.text: Lay your palm on the rope

effects.log: It is warm and trembling, and the trembling does not come from above.

choices.text: Let {npc} keep the second watch

effects.log: {npc} stays awake till the storm breaks and swears the rope sighed.

events.text: The rope does not end at the clapper. It runs through a neat bored channel in the floor, down through the old foundations, to a trap-hatch under the temple that nobody has opened in decades. {npc} holds the lantern with shaking hands. "Someone cut this," {he} whispers. "Someone built a bell that rings itself."

choices.text: Follow the channel with your fingers

effects.log: It runs down, not up. Whatever tolls the bell is beneath it.

choices.text: Put the hatch back exactly as it was

effects.log: Nobody must know you were here yet. {npc} helps, careful as a thief.

events.text: The temple's repair-rolls are dull until a single line: the masons who bored the channel were paid not from the temple's purse but from the Thunder Gate House storm-fund, with a note beside the sum: "Do not ask which orchard." {npc} reads it over your shoulder and goes pale.

choices.text: Copy the line out

effects.log: You copy it in your own hand. The note is the sort of thing a house hopes will be lost.

choices.text: Ask the mason-guild who signed

effects.log: The signer retired to a distant isle. The guild asks why you want to know, and you do not answer.

events.text: Below the temple floor, with {npc} holding the lamp, you find the secret storm gate: a bronze wheel in a stone throat, wired by a cord to the bell above. You lay it out: the Thunder Gate House opened storms over a rival's orchards unseen, and the bell tolled each time the gate was thrown. {npc} laughs once, shakily. "It was not haunted," {he} says. "It was rigged."

choices.text: Cut the cord and tell the temple

effects.log: The temple takes the cord down in an afternoon. The bell is silent in the next storm, and the orchards flower.

choices.text: Lay the case before the Celestial Ministries

effects.log: The Ministries seal the gate and the house is censured. Your name goes round the isles.

events.text: You named a ghost or a heart demon, and the temple takes it hard. The bell is wrapped in white cloth, and an old bell-keeper is blamed for a year of neglect. {npc} finds you after. "It was not a ghost," {he} says. "Ghosts do not use cord."

choices.text: Unwrap the bell yourself

effects.log: You take the white cloth off the great bell with your own hands. The temple watches.

choices.text: Go back to the rope

effects.log: Somewhere along the rope is the thing you missed.

events.text: A fall on the bell-tower ladder, a bad one in the dark. You come away bruised, and {npc} binds your arm with a strip torn from {his} own sleeve and scolds you the whole time.

choices.text: Let {npc} scold

effects.log: You let {him}. It is a kind of care.

choices.text: Insist you are fine

effects.log: You are not fine. {npc} knows it, and says nothing.

events.text: Nothing again. {npc} has begun to look at you the way a keeper looks at a bell that will not ring. "Perhaps we are asking the wrong questions," {he} says, carefully, and you hear what {he} does not say.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} would do

effects.log: {npc} tells you, at length. Some of it is good. You say so.

choices.text: Insist you are on the right track

effects.log: {npc} nods and says nothing more about it.

events.text: {npc}, a star-reader of the Star Sea Pavilion with ink-stained cuffs and a very steady voice, asks you to walk the observatory gallery. "One star on the great chart is wrong," {he} says, so low the gallery cannot hear. "A finger's width. Nobody else will measure. A seer's whole trade is being right."

choices.text: Measure it with {npc}

effects.log: You measure it against the real sky from the roof. The finger's width is real.

choices.text: Ask who else could have moved it

effects.log: "Seven seniors have the key," {npc} says. "Seven."

choices.text: Say a finger's width is a rounding

effects.log: {npc} nods politely and does not ask you again.

events.text: On the observatory roof, {npc} holds the great rim-chart against the real sky. Every star lines up but one, a finger's width off, and the pin that holds it is a shade brighter and sharper than the rest. {npc} breathes out. "Someone changed it in the last season," {he} says. "And did it carefully."

choices.text: Lift the pin and look at its seat

effects.log: The seat is clean, the paper behind it fresh. Whoever moved it did not hurry.

choices.text: Let {npc} copy the whole chart

effects.log: {npc} copies every star by lamplight. The copy will be right when the original is not.

events.text: The Pavilion's reading-log is a thick book of sealed entries. {npc} reads the one that matters aloud. The week the pin moved, only one reading was sold, to a House buyer: "a fortunate marriage in the eleventh star-hour". {npc} closes the book. "That star governs the eleventh hour," {he} says. "It was moved to make the reading true."

choices.text: Ask for the buyer's name

effects.log: A name of a lesser House, newly rich, newly eager for a marriage-seat.

choices.text: Keep the entry to yourself for now

effects.log: You say nothing yet. {npc} sees you keep the page.

events.text: A junior seer who keeps the Pavilion's pins finally talks over a cold lunch on the stair. "A senior asked for one star nudged for clarity," the junior says. "Paid in spirit-ink. I was told it was an adjustment. I did not ask whose." {npc} listens with both hands folded in {his} lap.

choices.text: Thank the junior and promise silence

effects.log: The junior looks as though a weight has come off. "Somebody had to ask," the junior says.

choices.text: Ask the senior's name

effects.log: "Senior Doyun," the junior whispers, and then looks as though that was a mistake.

events.text: At the Pavilion's morning gathering, with {npc} at your side, you set it out: a senior seer nudged one star to sell a House a fortune it had not earned, and a marriage was sealed on a false reading. The gallery is silent. Senior Doyun rises, bows once to the chart, and says only, "It was a small change."

choices.text: Ask the Pavilion to correct the chart and the marriage's record

mem.note: saw you right a false fortune

effects.log: The chart is re-pinned, the reading annulled. The two families, free of the false fortune, make their own choice.

choices.text: Let the Pavilion discipline its own

effects.log: The Pavilion suspends Senior Doyun for a decade. Your name goes round the isles as the reader who caught a star.

events.text: Your accusation of a rival pavilion goes out under the Pavilion's own seal, and a rival pavilion answers with a formal letter and a very cold bow. {npc} is quiet a long time. "A seer who guesses is a seer who is wrong," {he} says. "I put my name to it."

choices.text: Apologise to the rival pavilion

effects.log: You write a stiff, careful apology. It is accepted without warmth.

choices.text: Re-measure every star

effects.log: Measure by measure, you go over the chart again.

events.text: Weeks of cross-checking, and a bank of cloud rolls over the observatory the whole season. The sky stays shut. {npc} puts the lamp out and sits in the dark. "We wait for a clear night," {he} says. "The stars do not hurry for anyone."

choices.text: Agree to wait

effects.log: You write down what you have so far, so the waiting loses none of it.

choices.text: Chart what clouds do instead

effects.log: A small, odd study, but you learn the Pavilion's weather.

events.text: The Pavilion's sealed log is not meant for visitors, and a senior notices the page you opened. {npc} hears about it and winces. "Every door you knock on remembers the knock," {he} says.

choices.text: Send an apology and a gift of ink

effects.log: A small gift, an apology. It does not undo the cost, but it is noticed.

choices.text: Accept it and move on

effects.log: Some doors close. Others open. You go on.

events.text: {npc}, the postmaster of the Sky Post, sets a jade slip on the counter and does not let go of it. "It is addressed to you," {he} says. "By a name I have never seen you answer to. It has been going to the wrong isle every sixty years since before my teacher's teacher. I have a feeling I should stop sending it away."

choices.text: Hold out your hand for it

effects.log: {npc} lets go, slowly. The jade is cold and heavy, and the seal does not give.

choices.text: Ask how it kept coming back

effects.log: "The Post does not lose letters," {npc} says. "It misplaces them with great persistence."

choices.text: Say it must be meant for someone else

effects.log: {npc} puts the slip back on the shelf and does not argue.

events.text: On the Sky Post's dead-letter shelf, among a thousand slips lost in the cloud-mail, {npc} finds the one. It is addressed to a name you do not use, in a hand you almost know. The wax is old and cold, and the postmarks go back further than {npc} can read.

choices.text: Read the postmarks

effects.log: Each one is a different isle. Each one is sixty years after the last.

choices.text: Let {npc} keep it safe on the shelf

effects.log: {npc} moves it to the counter drawer, where the Post cannot misplace it again.

events.text: The Post's receipt-book is brown at the edges. The slip was posted from the foot of the White Stairs, prepaid for twelve redeliveries, by a hand that signs with a hooked downstroke. You know the stroke. You have used it all your life. {npc} sees your face and puts down the book.

choices.text: Press your own stroke beside it

effects.log: The hooked downstroke matches, to the hair. You hold the page very still.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to say nothing for now

effects.log: {npc} nods. The Post has kept stranger secrets.

events.text: You break the seal before a witness, with {npc} holding the lamp. Inside, in your own stroke: "If you read this, I am gone and you are new. Do not look for me. Look up." The date is the year before you were born. The last piece is not in this life: whoever wrote it knew a later self would have to be ready to hear it.

choices.text: Keep the slip, and the witness's word

effects.log: {npc} signs the witness-line and gives you a copy. "For whoever comes asking," {he} says.

choices.text: Burn a stick of incense for the one who wrote it

effects.log: The smoke goes straight up, which the Post-clerks call a good sign.

events.text: You are young, and have never stood in the Sky Post, and still your hand reaches for the dead-letter shelf. {npc} watches you take the slip down. "I was told you would come," {he} says. "Sixty years at a time, I was told, and each time a little less lost. Open it. I will not look."

choices.text: Open the slip

effects.log: In your own stroke, a short note. Your soul carried the question here. Now it can be answered.

choices.text: Ask {npc} who told {him}

effects.log: "The postmaster before me," {npc} says. "And the one before. It is on the shelf like a rule."

events.text: You say it aloud at the Post's counter, with {npc} listening: you posted the slip yourself, from the foot of the White Stairs, in the life before this one, to reach the self you would become. {npc} puts down the stamp. "Then the Post has delivered it," {he} says, smiling, "after all this time. It was always the right address."

choices.text: Send a reply, to no one in particular

effects.log: You post a short note to the future. {npc} stamps it and puts it on the right shelf.

choices.text: Keep the slip and thank the Post

effects.log: {npc} gives you the wax seal as a keepsake. The Post-clerks bow as you go.

events.text: "A forger," you said, or "a seer's slip of the brush," and the Post is loud with it. A clerk is questioned; a seer is shouted at in the arcade. {npc} looks at the slip a long time. "A forger would not pay for twelve redeliveries," {he} says. "Think again."

choices.text: Apologise to the clerk and the seer

effects.log: You go to each and say you were wrong. Most forgive you.

choices.text: Read the receipt-book again

effects.log: Brush-stroke, prepaid fee, the foot of the White Stairs. You read it till the lamp is low.

events.text: A month of asking after the slip's first post, and the trail ends at a post-office that was demolished a hundred years ago. {npc} brings you a cup of tea at the rubble. "Dead end," {he} says. "The Post is patient. So can we be."

choices.text: Wait

effects.log: You write down what you have so far, so waiting loses none of it.

choices.text: Walk the rubble once more

effects.log: Nothing new. But you now know every brick of it.

events.text: Word gets round the arcade that you are chasing a lost slip with your own name on it, and the teahouses enjoy it. Someone has written a comic ballad. {npc} hears it and goes red to the ears on your behalf.

choices.text: Laugh at the ballad too

effects.log: You laugh louder than anyone. The ballad loses its sting.

choices.text: Ignore it and keep going

effects.log: Let them sing. The truth does not care who is laughing.

events.text: The second wrong answer is the last. {npc} does not argue with you this time. {He} only gathers up the notes and copied pages, ties them with a cord of cloud-silk, and puts them in your hands. "Keep these," {he} says. "Someone will finish it someday. Maybe even you."

choices.text: Keep the bundle

effects.log: You keep it all. Perhaps a later life will open it.

choices.text: Give the bundle back to {npc}

mem.note: keeps the case for someone else

effects.log: {npc} takes it and promises to keep it for whoever comes next.

events.text: That is the second answer wrong, and the case is closed. {npc} unrolls the chart you kept together, looks at it a long while, and rolls it up again. "Some mysteries are patient," {he} says. "This one can wait for a better reader than either of us. Keep the thread. I will keep the door."

choices.text: Take the thread

effects.log: You tie the thread around your wrist. A later life may know what to do with it.

choices.text: Thank {npc} and go quietly

effects.log: You go, and {npc} stands at the door a long time.
